name: LM2596SX-5.0_NOPB
title: LM2596: 3 A, 150 kHz step-down switching regulator, 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and adjustable
summary: A monolithic buck regulator that switches an internal power transistor at a fixed 150 kHz and carries its own loop compensation, so a working supply needs only an input capacitor, a catch diode, an inductor and an output capacitor. It takes 4.5 V to 40 V in and delivers up to 3 A, in fixed 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions and an adjustable version referenced to 1.23 V (1.2 V to 37 V out). An active-low ON/OFF pin drops the supply current to about 80 µA, and the part protects itself with a two-stage current limit and thermal shutdown. It comes in a 5-pin TO-220 (several lead forms) and a 5-pin TO-263; the LM2596SX-5.0/NOPB is the 5 V version in the TO-263 on 500-piece tape and reel.

pins.name: +VIN
pins.function: Supply input of the regulator. Needs a low-ESR input capacitor right at the pin to hold down transients and deliver the pulsed switch current.

pins.name: Output
pins.function: The internal power switch: swings between roughly +VIN − VSAT and about −0.5 V at a duty cycle of about VOUT / VIN. Copper on this node is kept as small as possible to limit coupling into nearby circuits.

pins.name: Feedback
pins.function: Regulation sense input that closes the loop: tied to the output on the fixed versions, to the R1/R2 divider tap on the adjustable version.

pins.name: ON/OFF

circuits.title: Typical application, fixed output version
circuits.description: A 12 V to 5 V, 3 A step-down converter using the 5 V version. The internal switch chops the input onto the Output pin; L1 and COUT average it to 5 V, and D1 carries the inductor current while the switch is off. Feedback senses the output directly. ON/OFF is grounded, so the regulator always runs. CIN is the input reservoir.

circuits.title: Fixed output voltage version (Figure 20)
circuits.description: The general buck circuit for the 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V versions, with the parts of the design example. Feedback goes straight to the output node; ON/OFF is tied to ground. The input capacitor, ground pin, ON/OFF pin, catch diode and output capacitor all return to one ground; those connections and the switch-node loop carry the fast-changing currents and are kept short over a ground plane. The feedback wire is routed clear of the inductor's field.

circuits.title: Optional post ripple filter (Figure 20)
circuits.description: An LC stage after the regulator's output capacitor for very low output ripple: a 3 µH series inductor and a 180 µF low-ESR capacitor on short leads. It sits outside the feedback loop, so the capacitor's ESR can be as low as wanted.

circuits.title: Adjustable output voltage version (Figure 20)
circuits.description: The buck circuit for the adjustable version, also the test circuit for the electrical characteristics. R2 from the output and R1 to ground divide the output onto Feedback, which regulates at VREF = 1.23 V, so VOUT = 1.23 V × (1 + R2 / R1). CFF across R2 adds phase lead for stability when the output is high or COUT has very low ESR. R1 and R2 sit close to the Feedback pin on short leads.

notes: R1 is chosen between 240 Ω and 1.5 kΩ, about 1 kΩ, 1 % metal film.

circuits.title: Delayed start-up (Figure 33)
circuits.description: Holds the regulator off for a while after power is applied. While VIN is rising, C1 couples the rise onto ON/OFF through R1 and keeps the part off; once VIN settles, R2 discharges the node and ON/OFF falls below its threshold, starting the converter. R1 also limits the ON/OFF voltage, reduces noise pickup and limits C1's discharge current. Only the start-up parts are part of this circuit; Output and Feedback connect as in the normal buck circuit.
notes: A long delay is avoided when the input carries large ripple, which couples onto ON/OFF.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for buck regulator (Figure 34)
circuits.description: Keeps the regulator off until VIN reaches about the Zener voltage plus one volt. Below that, Q1 is off and R2 pulls ON/OFF up to VIN, holding the part off. When VIN drives current through R1 and Z1 into R3 and Q1's base, Q1 pulls ON/OFF low and the regulator starts.
notes: With a Zener above 25 V, an extra 47 kΩ from ON/OFF to the ground pin keeps ON/OFF within its 25 V limit.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for inverting regulator (Figure 35)
circuits.description: The same Zener-and-transistor lockout applied to the inverting circuit, where the regulator's ground pin and the lockout parts return to the −5 V output rail instead of system ground. D1 feeds the input. The ON/OFF threshold is about 13 V.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout with hysteresis for inverting regulator (Figure 36)
circuits.description: Lockout for the inverting circuit with the same parts and connections as Figure 35. The turn-on and turn-off points differ: switching starts at VIN = 13 V and stops at VIN = 8 V, a hysteresis about equal to the output voltage.

circuits.title: Inverting −5 V regulator with delayed start-up (Figure 37)
circuits.description: Makes −5 V from a +4.5 V to +20 V input. The regulator's ground pin rides on the negative output and Feedback is tied to system ground, so the part regulates the inverted output. L1 returns to ground; D2 is the catch diode. D1 keeps input ripple from reaching the output through CIN at light load and makes the loop behave like a buck. D3 stops the output being pulled more than a diode drop positive while CIN charges at power-up. C1, R1 and R2 delay start-up so CIN charges higher before the switch begins drawing its large start-up current.

circuits.title: Inverting regulator ground referenced shutdown (Figure 39)
circuits.description: Shuts down an inverting regulator from a logic signal referred to system ground. With the shutdown input at 0 V, Q1 is off and R1 holds ON/OFF at the regulator's ground pin (the −5 V rail), so the regulator runs. Taking the input to +V turns Q1 on through R4, pulling ON/OFF up and turning the regulator off.

circuits.title: Inverting regulator ground referenced shutdown using opto device (Figure 40)
circuits.description: Ground-referred on/off control of an inverting regulator through an opto-isolator. R1 and R2 bias ON/OFF high relative to the −5 V rail, so with the shutdown input at 0 V the regulator is off. Driving the input to +5 V lights the LED through R3; the phototransistor pulls ON/OFF down to the regulator's ground pin and the regulator runs. Input range +4.5 V to +25 V.

operation.text: A step-down (buck) regulator with the power switch, oscillator and loop compensation inside. It runs from up to 40 V and delivers up to 3 A of DC load current. Versions with a fixed 3.3 V, 5 V or 12 V output, and an adjustable version (1.2 V to 37 V, ±4 % worst case over line and load) are offered. A typical buck design needs four outside parts: input capacitor, catch diode, inductor and output capacitor. Output voltage tolerance is ±4 % over the specified line and load range, the oscillator ±15 %.

Inside are a 1.235 V reference, a 2.5 V internal regulator, a start-up circuit, an error amplifier with active-capacitor compensation, a PWM comparator driven by the 150 kHz oscillator, a latch and driver for the 3 A switch, two current-limit comparators referred to 220 mV and 200 mV across a sense resistor in the VIN path and a thermal limit. The fixed versions carry a feedback divider with R1 = 2.5 kΩ to ground and R2 = 4.2 kΩ (3.3 V), 7.6 kΩ (5 V) or 21.8 kΩ (12 V); the adjustable version has R2 = 0 Ω and R1 open, so Feedback goes straight to the amplifier.
The internal oscillator is fixed at 150 kHz nominal, which allows smaller filter parts than lower-frequency switchers. When the second stage of the current limit acts, the frequency is lowered.

ON/OFF is active low with a threshold near 1.3 V at 25 °C. Below it the regulator switches; above it (up to 25 V) the regulator stops and draws about 80 µA standby current. Tying the pin to ground or leaving it open leaves the regulator on. In the inverting configuration the ground pin sits at the negative output, so ON/OFF must be level-shifted from a ground-referred signal (Figures 39 and 40).

The output switch has a two-stage current limit, the second stage reducing the switching frequency; the peak current limit is 4.5 A typical. An overtemperature shutdown protects the part under fault conditions. Power dissipation is internally limited.

A capacitor from VIN to ON/OFF with a pull-down resistor (Figure 33) keeps the regulator off while the input rises and lets it start once the input is steady. This helps when the source can supply only limited current: the input can climb higher before the converter loads it, and a buck draws less input current at higher input voltage. Long delays are avoided when the input carries much ripple.

A Zener, a transistor and three resistors on ON/OFF (Figures 34 to 36) hold the regulator off until the input passes a set voltage, about the Zener voltage plus 1 V. One version has the same turn-on and turn-off point; the hysteresis version turns on and off at different input voltages, separated by about the output voltage (13 V on, 8 V off in Figure 36). With a Zener above 25 V, a 47 kΩ resistor from ON/OFF to the ground pin keeps ON/OFF under 25 V.

Connecting the ground pin to the negative output and Feedback to system ground makes a positive-to-negative converter (Figure 37); any output version can be used. The output current available depends on both input and output voltage (Figure 38). The input-to-ground-pin voltage is |VIN| + |VOUT| and must stay at or below 40 V. D1 isolates input ripple at light load and keeps the loop buck-like; a Schottky suits low input voltages and a fast-recovery diode higher ones. D3 limits how far positive the output can be pulled at power-up. The normal inductor procedure does not apply; 33 µH, 3.5 A suits most designs, and the Figure 37 capacitors work in most cases. At start-up the input draws up to the current limit (about 4.5 A) for at least 2 ms, until the output has settled, even at light load, so a current-limited source may fail to start it; the delayed start-up network and a larger input capacitor help.

The inductor selection guides give continuous-mode values. At low load currents (1 A and below) or high input voltages, a discontinuous design can use one half to one third of the inductance and a smaller part; peak switch and inductor currents rise but stay under the current limit. In discontinuous operation the switch pin shows damped ringing while neither switch nor diode conducts; this is normal, not loop instability, and carries little energy. Ferrite cores ring most, powdered iron less; a series RC across the inductor damps it.

A low-ESR aluminium or tantalum capacitor sits between VIN and ground, close to the part on short leads; it supplies the switch current pulses and stops input transients. Its RMS ripple current rating governs the choice more than capacitance: for up to 40 °C ambient about 50 % of the DC load current, for up to 70 °C about 75 %. The voltage rating is at least 1.25 × the maximum input; the design procedures use about 1.5 × for aluminium and 2 × for tantalum. Running above the ripple rating heats the electrolyte and shortens life. Solid tantalums can fail short if their surge rating is exceeded at turn-on; surge-tested types (AVX TPS, Sprague 593D) are preferred, or a series resistance or inductance ahead of them. Ceramic input capacitors can cause severe ringing at VIN.

The output capacitor filters the output and sets loop stability; low-ESR electrolytic or solid tantalum types made for switchers are used, judged mainly by 100 kHz ESR, then ripple current, voltage and capacitance. ESR has both an upper limit (ripple, typically 1 % to 2 % of VOUT) and a lower limit (very low ESR can make the loop oscillate). Electrolytics of 82 µF to 820 µF and tantalums of 10 µF to 470 µF work best; above 820 µF is not used. The voltage rating is at least 1.5 × VOUT, often higher for lower ESR. Electrolytic ESR rises about 3× at −25 °C and up to 10× at −40 °C, so below −25 °C solid tantalum is used. Tables 1 and 2 list working capacitors.

On the adjustable version a capacitor across R2 adds phase lead when VOUT is above about 10 V, when the input-output voltage difference is low, or when COUT has very low ESR (solid tantalum, for example). Values run from 100 pF to 33 nF (Table 2); ceramic, plastic or silver mica types are fine, Z5U ceramics are not.

The catch diode carries inductor current while the switch is off and sits close to the part on short traces. Schottky diodes are the first choice, especially at 5 V and below; ultra-fast recovery types (50 ns or less) also work, though some with abrupt turn-off cause instability or EMI. Slow rectifiers such as the 1N5400 or 1N4001 series are not used. Current rating: at least 1.3 × the maximum load, or the full current limit if the supply must survive a continuous short. Reverse rating: at least 1.25 × the maximum input voltage.

The selection guides (Figures 21 to 24) assume continuous conduction and size the inductor so ripple is a set fraction of the maximum load, a fraction that grows at lighter loads (Figure 28). Continuous mode gives more output power, lower peak currents and often lower ripple, but needs more inductance at light load or high input voltage; most designs go discontinuous at light load anyway. Open bobbin or rod cores are cheap but spread flux that couples into nearby traces and scope probes; with several switchers on one board, toroid or E-core parts are used. An inductor driven past its current rating overheats or saturates, its inductance collapses, and the switch is pushed into cycle-by-cycle current limit.

In continuous mode the output carries a sawtooth ripple at the switching frequency, typically 0.5 % to 3 % of VOUT, set by ripple current and output capacitor ESR, plus short spikes from the switching edges and capacitor lead inductance. For ripple below about 20 mV an LC post filter is added: 1 µH to 5 µH of low-resistance inductance and a low-ESR capacitor, outside the loop. Ripple is measured with a short probe ground at the output capacitor; a long ground lead distorts it.

Flux from an open-core inductor induces millivolts in nearby copper, which can raise ripple or upset stability. If an open-core part is suspected, lifting it away from the board shows whether its field is the cause; the remedies are a closed-core part or a changed layout. Flux crossing the ground, feedback or output capacitor traces matters most. A trace exactly centred under a bobbin inductor can be acceptable because the induced voltages cancel; off-centre it is not, and winding direction can matter.

The input capacitor, catch diode, ground and output capacitor connections carry fast-switching currents and are kept short and wide, over a ground plane or with single-point grounding, with all outside parts close to the IC. The Output pin keeps a small copper area. On the adjustable version both feedback resistors sit near the IC and their wiring runs away from the inductor, particularly an open-core one.

The TO-220 normally needs a heat sink, sized by input and output voltage, load and ambient (Figure 31 gives the rise with a heat sink at 3 A). The TO-263 tab is soldered to board copper that acts as the heat sink: at least 0.4 in², ideally 2 in² or more of 2-oz copper; beyond about 6 in² little more is gained (Figure 32 gives the rise at 2 A on 9 in²). Above 2 A, double-sided or multilayer boards with large copper areas, or airflow, may be needed. Generous copper everywhere helps except on the Output pin. The catch diode adds heat to the board; the inductor can add or remove heat.
